The Case for Radical Inheritance Reform: Why a Near-Total Estate Tax Deserves Serious Consideration

Introduction

The question of inherited wealth strikes at the heart of what kind of society we want to be. Does America truly believe in meritocracy—the idea that success should flow from talent, effort, and contribution? Or have we accepted a quiet aristocracy, where the circumstances of birth increasingly determine life outcomes? A robust inheritance tax, potentially approaching 100% above a modest exemption, represents one of the most philosophically consistent policies available to a society that claims to value equal opportunity.

This essay presents the strongest case for such a policy, engaging seriously with the arguments that have motivated thinkers across the political spectrum—from Thomas Paine to Theodore Roosevelt to contemporary economists—to question whether unlimited intergenerational wealth transfer is compatible with democratic ideals.

The Philosophical Foundation: Earned vs. Unearned Advantage

The Meritocratic Argument

The most powerful argument for limiting inheritance is simple: the heir did nothing to earn it. Whatever we believe about whether the wealthy deserve their fortunes, their children's claim to that wealth rests on nothing more than genetic lottery.

Consider the logic we apply elsewhere. We generally reject the notion that political office should be inherited. We abolished hereditary titles. We don't allow parents to transfer their professional licenses to children. In each case, we recognize that certain advantages should be earned rather than bestowed by birth.

Why should economic advantage be different? If we believe that rewards should flow to those who contribute—through work, innovation, risk-taking, or service—then massive inherited wealth represents a systematic violation of that principle. A child born to billionaires has done nothing more meritorious than a child born to minimum-wage workers. Yet one begins life's race at the finish line while the other starts miles behind.

The Liberal Tradition

John Rawls, perhaps the most influential political philosopher of the twentieth century, argued that inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society. Inherited wealth fails this test spectacularly. It provides enormous benefits to those who already enjoy every advantage while doing nothing for—and arguably harming—those at the bottom.

Even earlier, John Stuart Mill argued that inheritance beyond a "moderate independence" was unjustifiable. The liberal tradition, properly understood, has never endorsed unlimited property rights across generations. Property rights exist to encourage productive activity, not to create permanent dynasties.

The Economic Case: Efficiency and Growth

Misallocation of Capital

Contrary to intuition, limiting inheritance may actually improve economic efficiency. Currently, vast sums pass to heirs regardless of their ability to deploy capital productively. The mediocre grandson of a brilliant entrepreneur controls resources not because he can use them well, but because of ancestry.

A high inheritance tax would redirect capital toward its most productive uses. Wealth would flow to the public sector for investment in infrastructure, education, and research—areas with enormous positive externalities that private markets systematically underinvest in. Alternatively, it could be redistributed to citizens who would spend it, stimulating economic activity.

Encouraging Productive Behavior

Some argue that inheritance taxes discourage wealth creation. But the empirical evidence suggests the opposite dynamic may be more important: inherited wealth discourages productive behavior in heirs.

Research consistently shows that large inheritances reduce labor force participation and entrepreneurship among recipients. Why build something when you've already been given everything? Meanwhile, the prospect of leaving wealth to children may motivate some wealth creation, but plenty of other motivations exist—personal consumption, status, charitable legacy, the intrinsic satisfaction of building something valuable.

A 100% inheritance tax doesn't prevent wealthy individuals from enjoying their money during their lifetimes. It simply prevents them from creating a permanent dynasty.

Historical Evidence

Some of America's greatest periods of broadly shared prosperity coincided with high estate taxes. The top marginal estate tax rate exceeded 70% from 1940 to 1976, reaching 77% for the largest estates. This period saw the emergence of the great American middle class, high rates of economic growth, and social mobility that made the American Dream plausible for millions.

The subsequent reduction in estate taxes has coincided with—though not necessarily caused—increasing wealth concentration, declining mobility, and a fraying of the social fabric.

The Democratic Argument: Political Equality

Wealth as Political Power

In any realistic assessment of democracy, wealth translates into political power. The wealthy fund campaigns, hire lobbyists, own media outlets, endow think tanks, and generally shape the political environment in ways unavailable to ordinary citizens.

Concentrated hereditary wealth therefore threatens political equality. When the same families maintain economic dominance across generations, they accumulate not just money but political influence, social networks, and institutional control. This is not democracy; it is oligarchy with extra steps.

Thomas Jefferson, though himself a slaveholder with complicated views on equality, understood this danger. He proposed abolishing primogeniture and entail precisely to prevent the emergence of an American aristocracy. The question for us is whether unlimited inheritance, even without formal legal privileges, accomplishes the same aristocratic outcome through economic means.

The Corrupting Effect on Institutions

Extreme wealth concentration corrupts institutions beyond formal politics. Universities compete for wealthy donors, shaping research agendas and admissions accordingly. Media outlets respond to owner interests. Nonprofits cater to foundation priorities rather than genuine social needs.

Breaking up concentrated wealth across generations would distribute this institutional influence more broadly, creating space for a genuine marketplace of ideas rather than the agenda-setting power of a few wealthy families.

Addressing Counterarguments

"It's Their Money"

The most intuitive objection to inheritance taxes is that people should be free to do what they want with "their" money, including giving it to their children.

But property rights have never been absolute. They exist within a social context, enforced by a legal system that the community maintains. The notion that wealth is purely "yours," independent of the social infrastructure that made its accumulation possible, is a fiction.

Moreover, even accepting strong property rights for the living, it's not clear why these rights should extend beyond death. The dead have no interests. The inheritance question is really about what rights the living should have to receive unearned transfers, not about respecting the autonomy of the deceased.

"It Will Be Evaded"

Yes, wealthy individuals will attempt to evade inheritance taxes through trusts, gifts, and offshore structures. But this is an argument for better enforcement and broader base coverage, not for abandoning the policy.

We don't eliminate income taxes because some people cheat. We invest in enforcement and close loopholes. The same approach could work for inheritance: lifetime gift taxes at similar rates, strict rules on trusts, international cooperation on offshore assets, and penalties that make evasion costly.

"Small Businesses and Family Farms"

This objection has emotional resonance but limited empirical basis. With an appropriate exemption threshold—say, $5 million or even $10 million—the vast majority of small businesses and family farms would be completely unaffected.

For the small number of cases where genuine productive enterprises might be forced into sale, solutions exist: installment payment options, special valuations for operating businesses, or exemptions for assets that remain in active business use. The goal is eliminating dynastic wealth, not forcing the sale of productive enterprises.

"It Punishes Success"

This framing misunderstands what's being taxed. The successful individual is not punished—they enjoyed their wealth throughout their lifetime. Their children, who did nothing to earn the wealth, simply don't receive it. Calling this "punishment" requires believing that children are entitled to their parents' wealth, which is precisely the assumption being questioned.

"People Will Spend Rather Than Save"

Some argue that eliminating inheritance will cause the wealthy to consume rather than invest. But increased consumption creates jobs and economic activity. Meanwhile, the funds collected through inheritance taxes would be invested in public goods with high social returns.

Furthermore, many motivations for wealth accumulation beyond inheritance remain: security, status, power, the satisfaction of building, and charitable legacy. The ultra-wealthy are not primarily motivated by their children's fifth yacht.

Implementation Considerations

The Exemption Threshold

A reasonable exemption—perhaps $2-5 million—would ensure that middle-class families can pass homes and modest savings to children while capturing the dynastic wealth that creates aristocratic social structures. This exemption could be indexed to inflation and adjusted based on economic conditions.

Complementary Policies

An inheritance tax works best as part of a broader policy package:

  • Universal basic inheritance: Redistributing proceeds as a capital grant to all young adults, as proposed by Bruce Ackerman and Anne Alstott, would give everyone a stake in the economy.
  • Enhanced gift taxes: Preventing end-runs around the inheritance tax through lifetime gifts.
  • Strengthened charitable deduction rules: Preventing the use of "charity" as a vehicle for family control and social influence.
  • Investment in public goods: Directing revenues toward education, healthcare, infrastructure, and research that expand opportunity for all.

Transition Provisions

Implementing such a dramatic policy change would require transition periods and grandfathering provisions to allow adjustment and maintain basic predictability in the legal environment.

The Moral Vision

Ultimately, the case for a near-total inheritance tax rests on a moral vision of society. It asks: what do we owe each other, and what kind of society do we want to create?

The vision underlying inheritance reform is one where each generation starts reasonably fresh—where the accident of birth determines less and individual contribution determines more. It's a society where the children of janitors and the children of billionaires compete on something closer to equal terms, where talent and effort matter more than pedigree.

This is not a vision of enforced equality of outcome. Under such a system, enormous disparities would still emerge within each generation based on differential talent, effort, and luck. But these disparities would not compound across generations into permanent caste structures.

Theodore Roosevelt, hardly a radical, captured this vision: "The really big fortune, the swollen fortune, by the mere fact of its size, acquires qualities which differentiate it in kind as well as in degree from what is possessed by men of relatively small means. Therefore, I believe in... a graduated inheritance tax on big fortunes, properly safeguarded against evasion and increasing rapidly in amount with the size of the estate."

Conclusion

The case for a substantial inheritance tax—potentially approaching 100% above a reasonable exemption—is stronger than many assume. It rests on foundational principles that Americans claim to hold dear: that rewards should flow from contribution, that political equality requires limiting concentrations of private power, and that every generation deserves something like a fair start.

The practical objections, while real, are manageable with thoughtful policy design. The deeper resistance comes from accepting that we have a right to create dynasties—that birth should determine destiny.

Perhaps we will collectively decide that dynastic inheritance is a price worth paying for other values we hold. But we should make that choice explicitly, understanding its consequences, rather than treating unlimited inheritance as natural or inevitable. It is neither. It is a policy choice, and we can choose differently.

The American experiment was founded in opposition to hereditary privilege. Whether we extend that opposition to its logical conclusion in the economic sphere remains one of the great unfinished questions of our democracy.

Reasonable people disagree about inheritance policy, and compelling counterarguments exist regarding property rights, family values, incentive effects, and practical implementation challenges. The purpose here was to articulate one side of this important debate as forcefully and thoughtfully as possible.
